source: MAFF/GIZ, "Guidelines for Banana Export from Cambodia to China" (2022), section 1.3
text:
Since China granted market access for Cambodian banana in 2019, registered export-oriented banana planting area has expanded quickly, with the guide citing registered/company-scale growing area reaching into the thousands of hectares across more than a dozen provinces by 2020, and government and industry sources cited in the guide describing plans for further expansion toward considerably larger planted area and production volume in the coming years. Much of this growth has come from company-scale concession plantations (including foreign-invested agribusiness operations) growing Cavendish-type banana (Chek Ambong) specifically for export, alongside smallholder farmers who supply these companies under contract.

Importantly, the guide itself flags a specific agronomic risk tied to this rapid, geographically concentrated expansion: as new banana monoculture plantations multiply and cluster together in certain regions, the risk of Fusarium wilt (Panama disease) spreading increases, since dense single-variety plantings are exactly the conditions under which this soil-borne disease spreads most easily between neighboring farms. This is the same disease covered in agronomic detail elsewhere in the knowledge base (see the Fusarium wilt entries), and the export guide's warning underlines why disease-free planting material and field sanitation matter just as much for a farmer supplying an export-oriented company as they do for any other banana grower.
